questions.q: What is a cascade routing pattern?
options: Always sending every request to the largest available model
Trying a cheap, fast model first and escalating to a larger, more expensive model only when its answer isn't confident enough
Randomly selecting a model for each request with no logic
Running every model simultaneously on every request and averaging the results
questions.explain: Cascade routing tries the cheap model first and checks a confidence signal; only requests that fail to clear the bar escalate to the larger model, saving cost on the easy majority.

questions.q: In the example router code, what triggers escalation to the large model?
options: The small model's confidence falls below the configured threshold
The request arrives on a weekend
The prompt contains more than one sentence
Escalation happens on every single request regardless of confidence
questions.explain: The function checks draft.confidence against CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD; only when the small model's confidence is too low does the request escalate to call_large_model.

questions.q: Why add backoff and jitter to retries instead of retrying immediately and repeatedly?
options: Immediate repeated retries can turn one slow or failing model into a self-inflicted traffic storm that makes the problem worse
Backoff and jitter make retries happen faster
Jitter is required by law for all network requests
Retries without backoff are impossible to implement
questions.explain: Instant, repeated retries from many clients pile additional load onto an already struggling model. Increasing delay plus randomness spreads retries out and avoids amplifying the problem.

questions.q: What does a circuit breaker do once a model's failure rate crosses a threshold?
options: It permanently deletes the model from the system
It trips and stops sending new requests to that model for a cooldown period, routing to a fallback instead
It increases the retry rate to compensate
It automatically upgrades the model's hardware
questions.explain: A tripped circuit breaker stops hitting a failing model for a cooldown, protecting both the struggling model and the callers, then allows a few test requests through before fully reopening.

questions.q: Besides saving cost, what is the other main reason to route requests across multiple models?
options: Resilience — so a slow, overloaded, or down primary model doesn't cause every request to fail outright
To make every request take longer on purpose
Routing has no benefit beyond cost savings
To guarantee every request uses the exact same model every time
questions.explain: Routing also provides resilience: timeouts, fallback models, and circuit breakers mean a struggling primary model doesn't have to mean a failed request.
